#### **Betweenness Centrality $ g_{\nu}^{e} $: The Hidden Playmaker**

This is a more subtle but powerful concept. **Betweenness centrality** measures how often a player lies on

**shortest path** between other pairs of players.

Imagine the ball needs to go from the right-back to the striker. If it almost always goes through the central midfielder, then that midfielder has **high betweenness centrality**—they’re a critical bridge.

**Why is this important?**

A player with high betweenness is a **strategic bottleneck**. The team’s passing flow depends on them. That can be good (a creative playmaker) or risky (if the opponent marks them out of the game).

But here’s the key insight: **the distribution of betweenness across players** tells us about team structure.

- If one player has *much* higher betweenness than others, the team is **centralized**—it revolves around a single orchestrator.
- If betweenness is evenly spread, the team is **decentralized**—more collective, harder to shut down.

unpack what this equation is really doing. Imagine you’re trying to predict the outcome of a sports match—say, whether team $i$ will win, draw, or lose against team $j$ at time $t$. But you don’t know the teams’ true strengths. So instead, you look back at recent games and ask: *What set of team performance parameters would make the actual results we’ve seen the most probable?* That’s exactly what this formula is answering.

This is called **maximum likelihood estimation**—you’re searching over all possible parameter values (denoted by $\theta_{SM}(t+1) \in \Theta$) to find the one that *maximizes the total probability* (or "likelihood") of observing all the match outcomes that actually happened in the recent past—from time $t-d$ up to now, $t$.

- The outer sum, $\sum_{\tau = t - d}^{t}$, means we’re looking at the last $d+1$ time steps (e.g., the last 10 matchdays).
- $\Gamma(\tau)$ is the set of all matches that occurred at time $\tau$, so $(i,j) \in \Gamma(\tau)$ means “team $i$ played team $j$ at time $\tau$.”
- $P_{k(i,j)}^{i,j}(\tau)$ is the predicted probability of the actual outcome $k$ (win, draw, or loss) for that match, based on our current model.

So, we’re adding up how well our model predicts every recent game, and then adjusting the model parameters to make this total score as high as possible. Perhaps the key point about the results of this work is to evaluate the additional information that the time dependent game-averaged network measures provide to explain the final outcome of a match. Hence, despite the low values of $R^{2}$ and $\rho$ that the tournament-averaged network measures have with final position, the time varying game-averaged network measures seem to provide relevant and additional information about the outcome of games. For example, tournament-averaged vertex degree, excepting for the champion of the tournament, does not correlate well with the final rank in the tournament, while time varying game-averaged vertex degree seems to strongly influence the prediction success of games (see Fig. 3), which suggests that network variables do convey relevant information about the outcome of games. Game-averaged vertex degree provides the most statistical significant single variable determining the result of a game. This success is similar to the 50% success that it is obtained for the full model that combines all performance and network measures.

There are several additional factors that might be considered in this analysis, for example other network measures and non-linear effects. However, this work constitutes a first step to start uncovering the relation between time varying game-averaged network measurements and the result of a match. Other studies and improvements considering our methodology may be developed. For example, once the set of important variables has been identified, it could be possible to recreate possible scenarios using agents simulations $[26–28]$ , not only to forecast but also to have a better grasp of the football variables, the variability of the possible outcomes, and suggest ways to design and organize a team to confront a given opposing network. Such analysis will be included in future manuscripts.

It is worth mentioning that, because of the differences that may be found between the champion of the tournament of La Liga 20112–2013 (Barcelona F.C.) and the other teams, it opens the debate about considering information of other leagues and tournaments where teams are more similar in its performance and statistics. Moreover, other leagues may display other game styles in which passing networks may or not influence the forecasts.

Despite of being simple and widely used measures, vertex degree, betweenness centrality, and entropy provide a direct interpretation of our findings in the context of team strategies and soccer games. Our findings about the relevance of time varying game-averaged network measures may be correlated to soccer con-

cepts, one of the fundamental reasons why we use these particular measures. For example, betweenness centrality may be interpreted in terms of “game circuits”. For teams with lower mean betweenness centrality, players use different alternatives to move the ball, which means they do not only depend on one player or a couple of players. It may be interpreted also as a diversified passing team, something that intuitively, a team with a poor performance does not exhibit. It indicates the importance of a player or association between players in teams. As Fig. 1 shows, this implies that, for example Barcelona F.C. (statistically the team with the lower betweenness centrality), being the champion of the tournament, does not overload its passing network to force just a few interactions, but it diversifies the passing performance of the team. This fact may be contrasted with [19] arguing that Barcelona F.C. exhibits very different measurements that other teams. Similarly, vertex degree, gives information about the average number of passes or possession during a game, which by itself, seems to be the most significant determinant of the outcome of a game. Therefore, our results suggest strategies for coaches to design ways to confront a particular team.
Finally, it is important to note, from Fig. 3(B) and (C), that different combinations of variables do not convey linear contributions to the forecasting success. In some cases, considering additional information may improve the forecasting, but for some combination of variables that is not the case. Furthermore, we note that only for the network model we observe that there is a most efficient time window d beyond which the success decays.

Let’s unpack this carefully. First, the weights $W_{i,j}$ are assumed to be normalized so that $0 \leq W_{i,j} \leq 1$. This ensures they can be interpreted like probabilities—each edge represents a certain “likelihood” or “intensity” of interaction.

The core of the formula is the sum $\sum_{i,j} W_{i,j} \ln W_{i,j}$, which is the standard form of Shannon entropy. But notice the negative sign in front: since $\ln W_{i,j}$ is negative or zero (because $W_{i,j} \leq 1$), the negative sign makes the whole sum positive. The larger this sum, the more evenly distributed the weights are—meaning more uncertainty, hence higher entropy.

But there’s a normalization factor: $\frac{1}{N \ln(N - 1)}$. Why? Because entropy depends on the number of nodes $N$. Without normalization, larger networks would automatically have higher entropy, making comparisons unfair. This factor scales the entropy so that it ranges roughly between 0 and 1, allowing us to compare networks of different sizes.

So, in simple terms: if a team’s interactions are highly uneven—say, it plays very intensely with just a few teams—its contribution to entropy will be low. But if its interactions are more balanced across many opponents, it contributes to higher entropy, reflecting a more diverse and less predictable pattern of play.

These three measures—degree, betweenness, and entropy—each give us a different lens on team behavior. Degree tells us about activity level, betweenness about strategic positioning, and entropy about diversity of interactions. Together, they form a powerful toolkit for analyzing the invisible structure behind a football season.
